report:
## Conclusion

**The evidence strongly supports your claim.** Bystander hands-only (chest-compression-only) CPR is consistently associated with greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared to no bystander CPR. The American Heart Association states that immediate CPR can **double or triple** chances of survival after cardiac arrest. Multiple studies and meta-analyses confirm this benefit.

### Key Evidence

1. **AHA and general consensus**: The American Heart Association reports that immediate CPR can double or triple survival chances, and hands-only CPR is recommended for lay bystanders because it removes barriers (fear of incorrect technique, disease transmission concerns) that prevent people from acting at all. ([AHA CPR Facts and Stats](https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats))

2. **SOS-KANTO observational study**: This landmark study found that compression-only CPR resulted in a higher rate of favorable neurologic outcomes than standard CPR for patients with resuscitation starting within 4 minutes of collapse, and was clearly superior to no CPR. ([ScienceDaily summary](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2007/03/070315210134.htm))

3. **Meta-analysis**: A meta-analysis found that dispatcher-assisted chest compression-only bystander CPR is associated with improved survival after OHCA in adult patients. ([PMC Meta-Analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/))

4. **2025 review**: A recent review emphasizes that the bystander plays an essential role in the "chain of survival" for OHCA, where survival rates range from 2–22% globally. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S110996662400201X))

### Important Nuance

The evidence is slightly more complex for **children**: a meta-analysis suggested conventional CPR (with ventilations) may produce better outcomes for pediatric OHCA, likely because pediatric arrests are often respiratory in origin. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30391520/)) Additionally, hands-only CPR is at least as effective as conventional CPR for adults, and its simplicity increases the likelihood that bystanders will act rather than do nothing—which is the critical factor.
